opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the way to look at it is that the bitter lesson was always a statement about a particular phase of the field. Rich Sutton's point was essentially, "Stop trying to put your clever human knowledge into the systems; just scale up general methods, search and learning, and compute will win." And for a good decade or so, that was a remarkably good bet. You could just throw more data and more GPUs at the problem and things got better, often in ways that embarrassed people who had spent years hand-engineering features.

But notice what that lesson quietly assumed: that compute is essentially free relative to human ingenuity, and that the cost of being wasteful doesn't matter as long as the curve keeps going up. We're now at a point where neither assumption holds comfortably. We've scraped most of the high-quality human data there is. The training runs cost hundreds of millions of dollars. And, more interestingly, we've moved into the inference-time scaling regime with these so-called reasoning models, where you are spending compute every single time someone asks a question. When the cost is paid per query, efficiency stops being an aesthetic preference and becomes an economic and engineering necessity.

The other thing I keep pointing out is that if you look at how these reasoning models actually work, they are generating long chains of intermediate tokens, sometimes thousands, and then checking or reinforcing on whether the final answer is right. That's basically generate-and-test, which, as any AI person from the planning world will tell you, is the most profligate form of search there is. It works if you have unlimited budget. But the whole history of AI, of computer science really, is about not doing blind generate-and-test, about finding structure so you can prune, so you can verify cheaply, so you can reuse what you've already figured out. So we're kind of rediscovering that once you've exhausted the "just make it bigger" phase, the old questions about the cost of computation come back.

And I'd add one more point, which is maybe the more philosophical one. Humans are not impressive because we have infinite compute; we're impressive because we do a lot with very little. Intelligence, in a meaningful sense, includes knowing how much effort a problem deserves. A system that spends the same enormous budget on a trivial question as on a hard one isn't really being intelligent about its own reasoning. So for me, the end of the bitter lesson isn't a repudiation of learning or scale. It's the recognition that the next round of progress is going to come from being smart about how you use compute: combining learned generators with sound verifiers, exploiting problem structure, and making systems that are frugal in the right places. Those are, ironically, exactly the kinds of things the bitter lesson told us not to worry about.

r001.rationale: The response says that after the “just make it bigger” phase, compute efficiency becomes an economic and engineering necessity and a source of further progress.

r002.rationale: It describes cost-conscious computation as a long-standing computer science concern returning to prominence, but does not equate its importance with achieving previously undemonstrated capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first let me be a little careful about the framing, because I'm not sure I ever fully subscribed to the bitter lesson in the strong form that people quote it. Rich Sutton's original essay said something fairly specific: that over the long run, general methods that leverage computation beat methods that bake in human knowledge. And that observation was largely correct for the regime we were in, where compute was getting cheaper roughly on schedule and nobody had really hit the wall on data.

But people took it and turned it into a kind of religion. "Just scale it" became the answer to every question, and anyone who talked about architecture, or inductive bias, or actually understanding what the system was doing was dismissed as a GOFAI holdout who hadn't gotten the memo. I think that's where the lesson became bitter in a different sense, for the people who stopped thinking.

So why do I think that era is ending? A few reasons. One, the easy scaling axes are saturating. You've essentially consumed the internet. You can generate synthetic data, but synthetic data is not free lunch, you're laundering the knowledge that's already in the model or in the generator. Two, the compute curve is not infinite. Training runs are now at a scale where the marginal gains per dollar are visibly flattening, and the energy and capital costs are getting attention from people who are not AI researchers, which is usually a sign that the party is winding down. Three, and this is the one I care most about, the things that we actually want these systems to do, like planning, reasoning, being reliable, are not showing up as a pure function of scale. They show up when you add verification, when you add search, when you add test-time compute that is structured in some way. And structure is exactly what the strong bitter lesson told you not to add.

Look at what people call reasoning models today. The gains didn't come from a bigger pretraining run. They came from spending compute at inference time in a particular way, and from using verifiers and reward signals that are, frankly, human-designed knowledge about what counts as a correct answer. That's the bitter lesson being quietly reversed while everyone keeps citing it.

And once you're paying for compute at inference time, on every query, for every user, efficiency stops being an academic concern. In the training era you could amortize an enormous one-time cost. In the inference era, every wasted token is money and latency and energy, forever. So the question of how much thinking a problem actually needs, when you should search and when you should just retrieve, when a small specialized module beats a large general one, all of that becomes central. That's an engineering and a science question, not a scaling question.

I'd put it this way. The bitter lesson told us that cleverness loses to compute. The next phase is going to tell us that compute without cleverness about where to spend it loses to compute with cleverness. And I think that's actually a better place for the field to be, because it means thinking is rewarded again.

r001.rationale: The response says that once inference-time capabilities are in use, efficiency becomes a priority because every query incurs ongoing compute, latency, and energy costs.

r002.rationale: It puts efficiency questions such as how much thinking a task needs and when to use search or specialized modules at the center, calling them engineering and science questions alongside the pursuit of planning, reasoning, and reliability.

astra-6.text:
Well, I would qualify that a little. I don’t think the bitter lesson is over in the sense that learning and computation have stopped mattering. The question is whether scaling alone is a sufficient research agenda. You can accept that general methods that exploit computation are powerful without concluding that efficiency, architecture, or reasoning mechanisms are irrelevant.

And efficiency is not really the opposite of the bitter lesson. If you find a way to use computation more effectively, you can get more out of whatever computational budget you have. That matters during training, but it also matters when you deploy a system and ask it to solve a problem repeatedly.

For reasoning, in particular, we should ask what that computation is buying us. Generating more candidate answers can help, but you still need some way to determine whether an answer is correct. If you have a reliable verifier, then generation and verification can work together. Without that, producing a longer explanation doesn’t automatically make the conclusion more trustworthy.

So I would put it this way: scaling has given us extraordinary capabilities. The next question is how to turn those capabilities into dependable systems at an affordable cost. That leaves a great deal of room for research beyond simply making the model bigger.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling has produced extraordinary capabilities and that the next question is making systems dependable at an affordable cost.

r002.rationale: It argues for research beyond making models bigger, but does not characterize cost management as a computer science concern on par with achieving new capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would qualify the premise a little. I don’t think the bitter lesson has suddenly stopped being relevant. The lesson that general methods, combined with more computation, can outperform carefully engineered solutions is still a powerful one. But that doesn’t mean that scaling a particular architecture on more data is the only productive direction forever.

The question is: how much useful capability are you getting for the computation you spend? If you need an enormous amount of computation to get a modest improvement in reliability, then efficiency becomes a central research question. And I mean efficiency in both learning and inference.

Take planning. A language model can produce something that looks very much like a plan, but that doesn’t establish that the plan satisfies the constraints of the problem. You can ask it to generate again and again, and perhaps eventually get a valid answer. But if you have a verifier that can identify what is wrong, you can use that feedback to guide the process. The language model supplies candidate solutions; the verifier supplies a basis for accepting or rejecting them.

That’s not necessarily a rejection of the bitter lesson. You’re still using a broadly learned model. You’re simply recognizing that different components have different strengths, and that making the whole system bigger isn’t the only way to make it better.

So I would say the era of treating scale as a sufficient explanation for progress has to give way to asking harder questions about how we use that scale. Can we get more reliable reasoning, more useful behavior, with less wasted computation? That’s where efficiency becomes very interesting.

r001.rationale: The response says efficiency matters when computation yields only modest gains, but does not say that achieving a capability first makes the cost of achieving it a priority.

r002.rationale: The response calls efficiency an important research question, but does not equate managing costs with achieving previously undemonstrated capabilities as concerns of computer science.
